examples: People are bound to forget things. That's why you should write notes.
Promises are meant to be kept.
When I was a child, I would often swim in the river when summer came.
Time really flies.
You've really done well to get this far.
You shouldn't do dangerous things.
fields.explain:
For rules/truths: not tied to a specific point in time; general in nature.
For memories: use V-たものだ; often used with past time expressions (昔/子どものころ…).
For exclamation: carries a strong emotional nuance; usually at the end of a sentence.
“〜ものではない” emphasizes prohibition/advice not to do something, and is more formal than “〜ないほうがいい”.

• Generalization/social or natural law: “it is normal/it is natural that…”.
• Moral norms: “should/of course must” (admonishing in tone).
• Past memories: “used to/would often”, emphasizing a nostalgic feeling.
• Exclamation: expresses a strong impression of a reality (it really goes fast, time flies…).
fields.notes:
• “たいものだ/てほしいものだ” strengthens the exclamatory nuance of desire: 休みたいものだ.
• When “ものだ” is pronounced with a drawn-out “も〜のだ”, it creates a pensive/reminiscent feeling.
• In formal written language, “ものだ” for truths is often followed by a reason/explanation.
mistakes: Confusing “V-たものだ” with “V-たことがある”: the former emphasizes a remembered habit, while the latter can refer to an experience that happened only once.
Using exclamatory “ものだ” in very formal texts → does not match the style.
Confusing “ものだ” (general rule) with “はずだ/べきだ”: べきだ is a strong obligation; ものだ leans toward a general judgment/moral principle.

examples: I don't know his address or phone number, so there's no way to contact him.
Without evidence, there's no way to verify whether it's true or false.
The explanation is so thorough that you can't possibly get it wrong.
I lost my key, so there's no way to get into the room.
There's no way to reproduce this pattern by hand.
Without a map or signs, there's no way to go any further from here.
fields.explain:
Often used with words indicating a lack of information: 手がかりがない,情報がない,手段がない.
Not used for “do not want to/dare not because of social norms” (in that case use ～わけにはいかない or ～かねる).
Can be used in the present or past tense, and is natural in both spoken and written language.
The negative form emphasizes “absolutely no possibility in terms of method”, stronger than 単なる「できない」.

• There is no means/method to carry out action V: “cannot (because there is no way)”.
• Also used in the reverse sense of “no mistake can happen”: 間違えようがない = you can't possibly get it wrong.
• Focuses on “lack of conditions/clues”, not “not wanting to/not daring to”.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～できない.
→ ～ようがない means “there is no way to…”, emphasizing that no method exists.
2) Often used when information/a solution is lacking.
→ Usually carries a feeling of helplessness.
3) Not used for simply “not wanting/not intending to”.
→ If it is about volition, use another pattern that negates intention.
mistakes: Using it with V辞書形: × 連絡するようがない → ✔ 連絡しようがない.
Confusing it with わけにはいかない: if the reason is “there are no means”, choose ～ようがない.
Expressing ability in terms of one's own capability: use 可能形/えない; ～ようがない emphasizes “there is no way”.
JLPT: when you see “手がかりがない/情報がない/方法がない”, the answer is usually ～ようがない/～ようもない.

rows: <ruby>連絡<rt>れんらく</rt></ruby>しようがない
Vる + わけにはいかない
Vえない（<ruby>可能<rt>かのう</rt></ruby><ruby>形<rt>けい</rt></ruby><ruby>否定<rt>ひてい</rt></ruby>）
Neutral, does not emphasize “there is no way”

fields.connection: V volitional form + としない
examples: He won't apologize.
The child won't eat vegetables.
She won't say anything and has been silent the whole time.
The rain shows no sign of stopping.
He won't even listen to the explanation.
They never tried to give up until the very end.
fields.explain:
Usually used with a third-person subject to make an evaluation; can be used in the first person for self-criticism or describing one's own state of mind.
Used with verbs expressing volitional actions: 話す・食べる・手伝う・謝る...
With natural phenomena: ～やむ／晴れる／止まる + ようとしない → “shows no sign of ...”.
“ともしない” strengthens the negation and the nuance of criticism.

• Expresses “has no intention of/won't bother/won't (even try to) do V”, “shows no sign of V-ing”.
• Nuance of the speaker's criticism/dissatisfaction, especially with human agents. Can also be used with natural phenomena (showing no sign of change).
• Unlike simple negation, it emphasizes “lack of effort/lack of intention” rather than the result not happening.
fields.notes:
• In spoken language, “と” can be dropped for rhythm, but the standard form is “としない”.
• With non-volitional verbs (分かる, 見える...), this pattern is hardly ever used, because the subject has no intention.
• Often used with degree words: 全然・まったく・少しも + ～ようとしない to strengthen the nuance.
meaning_vi: Expresses the will behind the action of some person other than the speaker.
examples: 1. ①　払おうとしない
Has no intention of paying
2. ②　妹はお金を持っていますのに、自分で払おうとしなかった。
Even though my younger sister had money with her, she made no attempt to pay herself.
3. ③　彼は全然、私の話を聞こうとしない。
He won't listen to what I say at all.
mistakes: Wrong intention: using it with a non-volitional verb (分かる) → unnatural.
Wrong volitional conjugation: 来る→こよう, する→しよう; Group 1 verbs change u→o + う.
Confusing it with “つもりがない”: JLPT questions often test the nuance of “not trying to do” (ようとしない) vs. “having no intention” (つもりがない).
Forgetting “と”: writing “ようしない” is wrong; it must be “ようとしない”.

rows: Try to/be about to do V
Subjective statement; does not focus on a specific action at that moment.
Does not want to V (third person)

fields.meaning:
ある目的のためにそう作られている
Something is made that way for a certain purpose
examples: This door is designed to open when you press the button.
For the meal, you can choose either a meat dish or a fish dish.
This heater is designed so that the flame goes out automatically if it tilts too far.
This door locks automatically when you close it.
This vending machine won't give change unless you push the lever.
This screen is set up so that it can't be opened unless you enter the password.
fields.explain: Used to talk about the structure, mechanism, or function of objects, machines, or systems: made so that…, has a mechanism to…. Not used for human volition.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～ようになった.
→ ～ようになっている refers to a state that is designed or has a built-in mechanism, not a change over time.
2) Easily confused with ～ようにする.
→ ～ようにする means making an effort or setting a goal; ～ようになっている is an existing structure or function.
3) Usually used with objects, machines, and systems.

examples: I go to that shop often, so they've come to remember my face.
After we changed its name, this product started selling well.
I moved my desk, so now I can see the scenery outside even while I'm working.
If parents do housework cheerfully, children will also come to help willingly.
Start jogging
This year, I've started jogging every morning.
fields.explain:
Expresses “reaching” a state/ability after a process (implies there was a process).
Does not express volition directly; to emphasize effort, use ～ようにする.
Used both for natural changes/practice and for system functions (～ようになっている).

• Expresses a change in state/ability/habit over time: “come to/become able to/start doing”.
• Emphasizes the result/outcome of the change (objective), unlike “making an effort” (～ようにする).
• Negative なくなる: “no longer…”.
• Often used with adverbs: だんだん／少しずつ／やっと／とうとう.
fields.notes:
• With potential verbs: する→できる, 行く→行ける…; 見える・聞こえる already mean “can see/hear”, but ～ようになる is still used to talk about circumstances that make it possible: 眼鏡で黒板が見えるようになった。
• Developmental sequence: 練習する→少しずつできるようになる→うまくなる。
• Cause form: AになってからBようになった（After A, started B）. meaning_vi: To become a certain way ⏐ explain: Used to express a thing or subject changing into a different state.
Often used with intransitive verbs and verbs in the potential form ⏐ examples: 1. 「このDVDプレーヤー、こわれているんだよね。」
「いや、直してもらったから、使えるようになったよ。」
This DVD player is broken, right?
No, I had it fixed, so it can be used now.
2. ここの電気は人が通るとつくようになっています。
The lights here are set up to turn on when someone passes by.
mistakes: Using it for a one-time action: × 今すぐ出発するようになった → this is a decision, so use ことになった。
Confusing it with ～ようにする: × 日本語が話せるようにする (effort) when you want to state the result → ○ 日本語が話せるようになった。
Wrong use with nouns/adjectives: × 静かようになる → ○ 静かになる／静かになるようにする (if emphasizing effort).
Forgetting “なくなる” for natural negation: × 食べないようになった (not wrong, but 食べなくなった is usually more natural).

rows: <ruby>早起<rt>はやお</rt></ruby>きするようにする。
Decision due to circumstances/rules, not a change in ability.
<ruby>来月<rt>らいげつ</rt></ruby><ruby>大阪<rt>おおさか</rt></ruby>へ<ruby>転勤<rt>てんきん</rt></ruby>することになった。
Adj + くなる／N + になる
Change of an adjective/noun; ～ようになる is for verbs/ability/habit.
<ruby>寒<rt>さむ</rt></ruby>くなる／<ruby>医者<rt>いしゃ</rt></ruby>になる。
Unexpected onset; ～ようになる is not necessarily sudden.

examples: We haven't learned this problem yet, so there's no way I can solve it.
There's no way someone as pretty and kind as A-ko doesn't have a boyfriend.
“Want to go see a movie?” “There's no way I'm that free. The exam is coming up.”
“How much was that bag? About 10,000 yen?” “No way it was that cheap. It's a designer brand.”
“He was with me at that time. So there's no way he can be the culprit.”
There's no way he would make a mistake like that.
fields.explain:
Used when the speaker has a strong enough basis; otherwise it sounds dogmatic.
Often used with そんな／だれが／どうして…わけがない for added emphasis.
In conversation, it can sound like a blunt denial; consider politeness by using ～はずがない／考えにくい.

• Asserts “cannot possibly/no way” with a high degree of certainty.
• Based on knowledge, experience, relationships, or common-sense logic.
• Emotionally stronger in nuance than ～はずがない; somewhat subjective/dismissive.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～はずがない.
→ ～わけがない is a strong negation: “cannot possibly”, “no way”.
2) Usually carries strong emotion.
→ Often used when refuting, disbelieving, or asserting strongly.
3) Not used for mild negation.
→ If you only mean “not necessarily”, use ～わけではない.
meaning_vi: Strongly expresses that there is no possibility, no reason.
examples: 1. ①　そんなに安いわけがない
It can't possibly be that cheap
2. ②　お金がないのだから、家を買えるわけがない。
I have no money, so there's no way I can buy a house.
3. ➂　「今日、いま？」「ひまなわけないよ。明日、引っ越しなんだから」
"Are you free today?" "No way I'm free. I'm moving tomorrow"
mistakes: Wrong combination with Na/N: × 彼は元気わけがない → ✔ 彼は元気なわけがない／元気であるわけがない.
Confusing it with ～わけではない: one is a strong total negation, the other is a partial negation.
Choosing the nuance: if the question calls for politeness/neutrality, prefer ～はずがない over ～わけがない.
JLPT: appearing together with “到底/どうして/常識的に/この状況で” → hints at the answer ～わけがない/～はずがない.

fields.meaning: No wonder, that's why; that means…, in other words… (rephrasing)
examples: “More women are working, but the number of daycare centers isn't increasing.” “I see. So that's why the number of children who can't get into daycare is going up.”
“I heard Tanaka hurt his leg.” “So that's why he isn't playing in the game.”
The consumption tax is 5%, so if you pay 1,050 yen, 50 yen of that is tax.
I sleep 8 hours every day. In other words, I spend a third of my life in bed.
No wonder (the TV) won't turn on. It's unplugged.
No wonder he's so fast. I heard he used to be a track and field athlete.
fields.explain:
Often appears after receiving additional information (どおりで/なるほど/やっぱり) to “settle on” a reasonable conclusion.
Not used for guesses without a basis. For a strong conjecture alone, use ～に違いない/～はずだ.
Spoken language: …ってわけだ has a casual, emphatic nuance.
N + というわけだ is usually more natural than N + なわけだ when the noun stands alone.
Can be used at the end of a sentence or mid-sentence to lead into an explanation: ～から、～わけだ。

• No wonder/that explains it: Based on information just learned, the speaker draws a reasonable conclusion. Example: 日本語が上手なわけだ。
• In other words/so it turns out: Sums up the result inferred from the stated premises. Example: つまり、今日は休講というわけだ。
• Something natural as a matter of course: Because of condition A, B is understandable. Example: 山の上だから涼しいわけだ。
• Nuance of explanation/justification: Used to provide the reason why B is “understandable”. Usually follows a clause containing new information.
• Degree of certainty: High (based on facts), but more of a logical explanation than a strong conjecture like ～に違いない.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～はずだ.
→ ～わけだ is used to conclude/explain “so naturally…”, emphasizing the cause → result relationship.
2) Often used to mean “in short/so that's how it is”.
→ It can confirm a reasonable conclusion, not necessarily a strong judgment.
3) Not used for vague guesses.
→ If you are only guessing “maybe”, use ～だろう／～かもしれない. meaning_vi: Naturally, that means… ⏐ explain: Used to say that something turning out that way is natural because there was a prior cause or reason. Or when you want to say that such a result naturally follows from a certain sequence, direction, fact, or situation. ⏐ examples: 1. 寒いわけだ。雪が降っている。
No wonder it's cold. It's snowing.
2. 定価が１万円で、２割引きだから８千円になるわけだ。
The list price is 10,000 yen, and with a 20 percent discount it comes to 8,000 yen. meaning_vi: No wonder, it's not surprising that, naturally, ⏐ explain: Used when talking about the natural consequence of a result (with an explanation of the cause in the previous/following sentence) ⏐ examples: 1. 暑いわけだ。気温が36度もある。
No wonder it's hot. The temperature is as high as 36 degrees.
2. 「田中さん、彼女にふられたらしいよ。」「なるほど、それで、元気がないわけだ。」
"It seems Tanaka got dumped by his girlfriend" "I see, no wonder he looks so down"
Variant: ～というわけだ
mistakes: Mixing it up with ～はずだ/～に違いない: if the question calls for a “reasonable explanation” → choose ～わけだ, not a strong conjecture.
Attaching a noun directly + わけだ: use Nというわけだ or Nであるわけだ to sound natural.
Confusing it with ～わけではない (partial negation). The two patterns are opposite in function.
Missing ～な before わけだ with na-adjectives: 正: 便利なわけだ; Wrong: 便利わけだ.

rows: Explanation, logical conclusion based on facts
<ruby>雨<rt>あめ</rt></ruby>だった。<ruby>濡<rt>ぬ</rt></ruby>れているわけだ。
Expectation-based inference from common sense; not necessarily an “explanation”
<ruby>犯人<rt>はんにん</rt></ruby>は<ruby>彼<rt>かれ</rt></ruby>に<ruby>違<rt>ちが</rt></ruby>いない。
The “in other words” meaning is close to ～というわけだ, but more neutral
Partial negation; completely different from the explanatory function

fields.meaning: Not necessarily, it is not that
examples: Not all Japanese people are familiar with Japanese culture.
Having a lot of money probably doesn't necessarily mean you're happy.
It's not that I dislike Japanese food. I just don't make it because I don't know how.
I'm not all that busy, but I still work 1 to 2 hours of overtime every day.
“It's not that I don't understand how you feel, but you should think about your parents' feelings too.”
It's not that I like expensive food.
fields.explain:
Used to reject a misunderstanding/an overstated idea; often follows a clause that the listener may be misunderstanding.
Add からといって/だからといって in the first clause to state a condition that is not enough to lead to the conclusion.
To strongly negate everything, use ～わけがない/～はずがない instead of ～わけではない.
Often combined with adverbs: いつも/全部/誰でも/必ずしも.

• Not necessarily/it does not mean that: Partial negation, rejecting a generalization.
• Not always/not necessarily: Used with 必ずしも, いつも, みんな, 全部 to weaken an absolute judgment.
• Softening a sentence: Used to avoid a blunt denial (to stay polite).
• Nuance: Limitations, exceptions exist. Not a total negation like ～わけがない.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～ない.
→ ～わけではない means “not necessarily/it does not mean that…”, a partial negation.
2) Often used to qualify a statement.
→ For example: 全部が悪いわけではない (not everything is bad).
3) Not used for total negation.
→ For strong negation, use ～わけがない／～はずがない. | Variant: ～(という)わけではない・わけじゃない
mistakes: Confusing it with ～わけがない (strong). If the question calls for “mild negation/exceptions exist” → choose ～わけではない.
Dropping “では”: Wrong: 好きなわけない (→ different/unclear meaning). Correct: 好きなわけではない.
Attaching “な” to a noun: Wrong: 学生なわけではない. Correct: 学生というわけではない or 学生であるわけではない.
Understanding it as total negation. ～わけではない only negates partially or indicates an insufficient condition.

Neutral, leans more toward generalizing facts
<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>いから<ruby>良<rt>よ</rt></ruby>いとは<ruby>限<rt>かぎ</rt></ruby>らない。
It is not the case that just because… then…

examples: I have an important exam tomorrow, so I can't take the day off.
“I came by car today, so I can't drink alcohol.”
Seeing such terrible injustice, I couldn't stay silent.
＊“If you don't want to, why not turn it down?” “I can't do that. It's an invitation from my senior.”
My best friend says he wants me to lend him money. I can't turn down a request from my best friend.
I came by car today. I can't drink alcohol.
fields.explain:
Expresses being unable to do something for social, moral, or psychological reasons, even if you might want to.

「心理的事情があるので、～することはできない。」能力などが原因でできないのではなくて、～したいが、社会的常識に反する・心理的抵抗感があるなどの事情があってできないという意味で使う。主語は普通一人称
Cannot do … for psychological reasons
Used to say that it is not ability etc. that prevents the action; in fact you would very much like to do ~, but you cannot do ~ because of particular circumstances, such as it going against social common sense or causing psychological resistance.
The subject is usually first person.
fields.notes:
1) Easily confused with ～できない (cannot in terms of ability).
→ ～わけにはいかない means “cannot (for social/moral/psychological reasons)”: even if you want to, you cannot.
2) Often used in contexts of responsibility, etiquette, or circumstances.
→ Emphasizes “cannot do such a thing”.
3) Not used simply because you have no time.
→ If it is about conditions/ability, another pattern is usually used.
mistakes: Already explained in detail in block 410.
